newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Solana to face Russian resistance on Moscow visit.
newsitem.headline: Solana to face Russian resistance on Moscow visit.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana travels to Moscow on Sunday, but will find it hard to convince Russians to drop their stubborn opposition to an expanded alliance.

Solana arrives with a package of measures aimed at softening the blow of NATO's planned expansion into eastern Europe, including a promise of a permanent consultative forum between the two former foes.

But Russians across the politial spectrum are alarmed at the thought of countries Moscow viewed as Cold War satellite states joining the Western alliance. Officials know there is little they can do against the plans, but they are still concerned.
"The question of broadening the alliance is threatening to become the main headache for Russian diplomacy in the coming years," the influential Izvestia newspaper said on Saturday.
A government foreign policy expert said officials were concerned that little might emerge from Solana's visit.

"We are slightly worried that Solana will come here as an American evangelist rather than as a negotiating partner," he said. "We are looking for a deal which would guarantee our national interests rather than verbal assurances that everyone is Moscow's friend."

Russian officials have spoken out frequently against NATO's plans to expand eastwards, which they say could threaten Russia's national security. A final NATO decision on what to do is likely at a summmit meeting in July.
"If NATO wants to expand let it expand, but we are against this," Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said last week.
Asked if he saw NATO's expansion as a danger to Russia, he said: "Russia faces potential threats from the west, south and east...But these are potential threats, not enemies."

President Boris Yeltsin is also opposed to the expansion plans. But a bout of pneumonia has put him in hospital for over a week, freezing political activity at home and raising questions about his ability to see out his four-year term of office.

Solana, asked by the alliance to negotiate a treaty or a charter with Moscow, is due to hold some five hours of talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov at a government dacha outside Moscow on Monday.
But the two men will meet behind closed doors and Russian officials said it would take more than five hours to iron out all differences between the two sides.
"All the questions for Russia and NATO will not be solved at a single meeting, even a five-hour one," Interfax news agency quoted a senior foreign ministry official as saying.
"We do not plan to invite the press to the talks in order to give both sides the chance of working as effectively as possible," the official added.

NATO has already said it would not station nuclear weapons on the territory of the first new members, widely expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, and hinted it would make the same commitment for conventional forces.
Independent Russian analysts say Moscow is keen to win as many concessions as possible before NATO enlargement goes ahead.
